gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the Baseus PicoGo AM52's "10,000 mAh" is a 36 Wh pack against 39.2 Wh for the Anker MagGo 2 Pro's "10,000 mAh", and that per Wh the two refill an iPhone equally in Macworld's test (5.06 vs 5.08 points per Wh), so the Baseus's lower score (182% vs 199%) comes from the smaller cell and it costs about $31 per full iPhone refill against about $55 for the Anker.
standout_why: Compared against Macworld (cited), which I read in full except its recharge-test methodology section. Macworld already prints Wh and a recharge score for each pack and says mAh is a blunt measure, so the raw inputs are on a cited page. It does not divide score by Wh or by price, does not point out that the AM52 is the only 36 Wh pack among the 39.2 Wh ones, and does not say the 45 W in the AM52's name is output only (its chart lists 30 W input). TechRadar (cited) returned only its title and The Verge (cited) could not be fetched, so neither was compared. pickedtech.com failed on a certificate error. Macworld does not cover the two cheapest picks in the ChatGPT answer (INIU SnapGo Compact P771, UGREEN MagFlow 10000 non-Pro).
decides: Confirms ChatGPT's pick of the Baseus AM52 for everyday use, with a correction to how it is described: it holds about 8% less energy than the Anker, not the same "10,000 mAh". The Anker MagGo 2 Pro's premium buys speed and a faster refill of the pack itself (45 W input vs 30 W; maker claim of 0-50% on an iPhone 17 Pro in about 25 minutes vs INIU's maker claim of 33 minutes on the same phone), not more charge per Wh. The INIU SnapGo Compact at $44.99 stays the budget pick on price and the maker's "1.8 phone charges" claim alone; no independent score was read for it.
